transcript:
[00:00] Ethan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on — I'm Ethan, AE at Redwood. Maya's our solutions engineer. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Raj (Converge): Raj here, lead backend. Ava and Sophie are here too.
[00:10] Ava (Converge): Hi all.
[00:12] Sophie (Converge): Hi.
[00:15] Maya (Redwood): Awesome. High level today: we'll show a short python + ts quickstart, auth patterns, then jump into Optimize tips and the devstack setup. We'll keep it very hands-on. Sound good?
[00:28] Raj: Yep, our main goals are: one, get something in CI that runs reliably; two, keep patient data off public endpoints; three, measure latency for a 512-token clinical prompt.
[00:38] Ethan: Totally. We'll highlight both hosted API for quick onramp and the private/Dedicated options if you need VPC. Quick question — are you leaning cloud-hosted or on-prem?
[00:48] Ava: We're evaluating. Compliance wants private control plane but product team wants quick dev velocity. So maybe start hosted with data segregation then move to private if needed.
[00:59] Maya: That makes sense. For hosted you can use token-scoped keys + per-route RBAC; for Private we support VPC peering and customer-managed KMS. Note: some transcriptions later call keys "KMS KMS" — ignore that.
[01:14] Sophie: About auth — we use Okta for SSO; can we map to Redwood roles?
[01:20] Ethan: Yes, we support SAML/SSO and SCIM provisioning; you can map Okta groups to RBAC roles in the console. We'll send the SSO guide in the doc link.
[01:27] Raj: Great. Can you walk the quickstart repo?
[01:30] Maya: Sure. Screen share — I'll open the sample repo. (screen share noise) You'll see root/README.md, examples/python, examples/ts, and a .env.example. The python quickstart shows installing redwood-sdk via pip, set REDWOOD_API_KEY in env, and run small script that calls client.generate.
[01:52] Maya: Note: in the python example we demonstrate streaming and non-streaming. For streaming we use websocket-ish streaming helper — sometimes transcribed as "web sock helper" — it's a small helper.
[02:05] Raj: For CI we store secrets in our vault. Are there best practices for rotating keys?
[02:10] Ethan: Yes — rotate regularly, and we support short-lived keys via our token service. You can also integrate KMS so Redwood never stores plaintext keys; we can provide the flow for that.
[02:20] Ava: On the private side — latency to our on-prem cluster is a concern. Does Redwood support collocated inference?
[02:26] Maya: We have a Private deployment package that ships with a control plane you can host in your VPC. For very low latency we recommend Dedicated pools or on-prem nodes; we can size based on your concurrency. Also Auto batching will try to keep per-token cost low, but that affects tail latency, so it's a tradeoff.
[02:45] Raj: Could you show how batching configs look in the repo?
[02:48] Maya: Yep — under optimize/playbooks there's a suggested batching.json and a small script that runs a micro-bench with different batch sizes and reports latency and cost.
[02:58] Ethan: Quick callout — Optimize recommendations are heuristics built from your p95 latency targets and token distribution. They might recommend quantization to int8 for cost but that can change output nuance; we log quality regressions tied to eval suites.
[03:15] Sophie: How do we set up evals?
[03:18] Maya: We have a small eval harness in the repo: tests/evals/*. You can point those to a prompt set and Redwood will run periodic regression checks. We'll share a template.
[03:30] Raj: About data retention and audit logs — our security team wants immutable audit trails for inference requests.
[03:36] Ethan: We provide audit logs with timestamps and token-level usage. For private you can keep logs on your side; for hosted we can push logs to your logging endpoint or store with configured retention.
[03:46] Ava: Is the data encrypted at rest with our KMS?
[03:50] Maya: Yes, in Private and Dedicated you can use your KMS/HSM. For hosted we use our managed encryption but offer a bring-your-own-key option in enterprise plan.
[03:59] Raj: Ok, demo time — can you run a python quickstart?
[04:02] Maya: Running now. (typing) Script calls client.generate with model: redwood-base-3b, input: 512-token clinical summary, max_tokens: 512.
[04:22] Transcription note: Maya's voice got clipped mid-sentence — weird.
[04:26] Maya: The sample returns in about ~120ms per token in this demo env — that's synthetic; in your env we expect different numbers.
[04:37] Raj: What's the expected p95 for a 3b model on dedicated?
[04:40] Ethan: On dedicated GPUs with proper batching and KV cache warm, p95 is typically 80-120ms for 512 tokens incremental generation; but it depends heavily on sequence length and hardware. We'll share performance matrix.
[04:57] Ava: Are there tooling hooks for tracing? We use Datadog.
[05:01] Maya: Yes — you can forward traces; we have tracing hooks and token-level timelines in the Console. We send spans to Datadog via OTLP. (slight background noise)
[05:12] Sophie: Regarding cost — what's the delta between hosted and dedicated per token?
[05:16] Ethan: Hosted is usage-based and easier to start; dedicated gives much better unit economics at scale. Our Optimize tool will estimate costs for your token mix and recommend dedicated sizing if it recoups within N months. We'll attach a sample calc.
[05:32] Raj: Any gotchas on TypeScript example we should know for Next.js?
[05:37] Maya: Put API keys server-side only. For Next.js we recommend server components or API routes — don't expose keys in the browser. Also the ts example includes an edge-friendly client for streaming. Some transcriptions call it "edge fahendly" — ignore.
[05:52] Ava: On the security front, legal wants a list of subprocesses that Redwood runs on dedicated instances.
[05:58] Ethan: We'll send a sanitized process list and the SOC2 artifact. For Private we'll provide on-prem docs.
[06:06] Raj: Can you explain the KV cache and warm-up behavior? We have a lot of short prompts and worried about cold start.
[06:12] Maya: KV cache stores past key-values for decoder layers; warm-up is important for multi-turn contexts. For many short requests we recommend prefix caching and micro-batching; Optimize can recommend prefix cache TTLs. Note: transcript sometimes writes KV as "kid V" erroneously.
[06:30] Ethan: Do you have a target date for the POC?
[06:33] Sophie: We'd like to kick off before year-end if possible — ideally week of Dec 18.
[06:37] Ethan: Good — we'll aim for 12/18. Action items in the notes.
[06:42] Maya: Quick live check — I'm going to open the CI snippet real fast. (typing) Here's an example GH action that pulls REDWOOD_API_KEY from your secrets vault and runs tests against the sandbox.
[06:58] Raj: Nice. For the sandbox keys, do they expire?
[07:01] Ethan: We can issue short-lived keys for the trial; they expire and you can rotate.
[07:07] Ava: Anything special for HIPAA?
[07:10] Ethan: For HIPAA workloads we recommend Private with dedicated storage and BYOK (bring your own key). We can sign BAA upon legal review.
[07:19] Sophie: Ok. Anything about model rollouts and automatic fallback? We need predictable behavior if a model has issues.
[07:24] Maya: Rollouts support canary and A/B. You can configure automatic fallback to a smaller model on error. Also you can pin model versions in routes. We'll show an example in the Console.
[07:37] Ethan: Quick note — people often confuse canary policies with traffic split; ours supports both weighted and metric-triggered rollbacks.
[07:47] Raj: Great. Any deeper infra questions we should prepare for the POC?
[07:51] Ava: We'll need to confirm VPC peering windows and firewall rules. Also port ranges for inference cluster.
[07:57] Maya: We'll send a network checklist.
[08:00] Ethan: Ok, let's do a short recap and next steps.
[08:04] Maya: Recap: Redwood to share sample repo + sandbox keys, security docs (SOC2, BYOK notes), Optimize playbook, network checklist. Converge to confirm peering windows, provide CI secrets pattern, and schedule POC kickoff.
[08:20] Sophie: Sounds good.
[08:22] Raj: Thanks everyone.
[08:25] Ethan: Thanks, we'll follow up with the links.
[08:29] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription quality: there are several short clipping artifacts and a couple of mis-heard technical terms (e.g., "web sock helper", "kid V cache"). Speaker labels are mostly correct. The body above contains the important dialog, action items, and next steps.
